title: CAN YOU LUST AFTER YOUR OWN SPOUSE?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LUST AFTER YOUR OWN SPOUSE?

The question Christians whisper about but rarely dare to ask—and the biblical answer may confront both the ashamed spouse who thinks desire is dirty and the selfish spouse who has mistaken desire for love.
There is a question some married Christians are almost embarrassed to ask.
They love Jesus.
They love their spouse.
They want their marriage to honor God.

And yet somewhere between purity sermons, warnings about lust, painful histories, pornography-saturated culture, and the awkward silence that often surrounds sexuality in church, they began wondering whether even wanting their own husband or wife too intensely might somehow be sinful.
So the question comes quietly.
Can I lust after my own spouse?
And behind that question there is often another one:
Is God disappointed in me for strongly desiring the person I married?
But there is another spouse asking the same question for a very different reason.
That spouse isn't afraid of desire.
That spouse may be using "marriage" as permission to become demanding, degrading, coercive, porn-shaped, selfish, or entitled.
One person needs freedom from false shame.
The other needs freedom from selfishness.
Both need Jesus.
And Scripture gives us something far more beautiful than the simplistic answers of either "sexual desire is dirty" or "anything goes because you're married."
The Bible gives us holy desire.
Desire shaped by covenant.
Desire governed by love.
Desire that sees a spouse not as a body to consume, but as a person to cherish.
And that distinction changes everything.
When Jesus speaks His famous words about lust in Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads in part:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn

In context, Jesus speaks of looking at a woman with the purpose of desiring her and says that such a person has already committed adultery with her in his heart. The key verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, set one's desire upon, and depending upon context, covet or lust. Matthew then explicitly frames the offense as adultery of the heart.
That matters enormously.
Because desire itself is not automatically sinful simply because it is strong.
The moral character of desire depends upon what is desired, why it is desired, and what that desire is doing to another human being in your heart.
Scripture does not command husbands and wives to become sexually indifferent toward each other after the wedding.
Quite the opposite.
Proverbs 5 tells a husband:
"Rejoice with the wife of thy youth."
And then Scripture becomes astonishingly physical:
"Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love." — Proverbs 5:18–19, KJV.
Read that again.
Slowly.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
We are.
Sometimes church culture has been.
Sometimes wounded people understandably have been.
But Scripture isn't.
Proverbs does not tell the husband merely to tolerate his wife sexually.
It tells him to delight in her.

The Hebrew imagery is intentionally passionate. The language translated "ravished," "captivated," or even "intoxicated" in various translations communicates being deeply carried away by her love. The NET translators explicitly understand the passage as directing sexual pleasure toward the marriage relationship and describing such delight as God-given.
That destroys one dangerous lie immediately:
Being sexually attracted to your spouse is not inherently sinful.
You do not need to repent because your husband's touch still affects you.
You do not need to feel dirty because you look at your wife and desire her.
You do not become more spiritual by becoming less affectionate toward the person with whom you entered covenant.
The Song of Songs makes that nearly impossible to argue.

It contains mutual longing, admiration, physical attraction, anticipation, delight, vulnerability, and romantic desire. Biblical scholarship has long recognized the Song's extraordinary treatment of reciprocal love and sexual longing; it gives voice to both lovers rather than portraying desire as belonging only to the man.
There is something breathtaking about that.
God could have given humanity a Bible in which married lovers never noticed each other's bodies.
He didn't.
He gave us the Song.
And yet...
Here is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
Because while you may rightly desire your spouse, it is possible to treat your spouse lustfully in the sinful sense Christians usually mean when they use that word.
Not because marital attraction becomes adultery simply by becoming intense.
But because sinful lust is ultimately about more than attraction.
It can become desire severed from love.
Desire severed from honor.
Desire severed from faithfulness.
Desire severed from the good of the other person.
It is possible to be married to someone and still reduce them in your heart to what their body can provide you.
It is possible to touch someone without truly seeing them.
It is possible to share a bed while becoming emotionally miles apart.
It is possible to say...
"You're my wife."
"You're my husband."
...while forgetting the more important truth:
They belong first to Christ.
Your spouse is not merchandise purchased by a wedding ring.
Not an appliance for relieving desire.
Not a performer.
Not a body whose boundaries stopped mattering when vows were exchanged.
Not a substitute for pornography.
Not someone required to reenact whatever the world taught you sexuality was supposed to look like.
This is where Christian marriage becomes radically different from consumption.
The world often teaches:
I desire you because of what you can do for me.
Christ teaches us to love by asking:
How can I seek your good?
That does not kill passion.
It redeems it.
And Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 7 are remarkable precisely because they are mutual.
The Greek of verse 3 says:
τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί

The husband is instructed to give his wife what is due within the marital relationship, and likewise the wife toward her husband. Paul continues by describing marital bodily authority reciprocally: he does not give unilateral sexual ownership to the husband; he astonishingly speaks in both directions.
That word "likewise" matters.
Christian intimacy is not supposed to look like one person taking while another person disappears.
The Gospel does not train us to ask, How much can I demand?
The Gospel creates people who ask, How deeply can I love?
And Hebrews gives us another breathtaking sentence:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
"Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled..." — Hebrews 13:4.
Notice the two realities standing together.
Marriage is honorable.
The marriage bed is to remain undefiled.
Scripture refuses both extremes.
It refuses the lie that marital sexuality is inherently filthy.
And it refuses the lie that marriage magically makes every sexual attitude holy.
The bed belongs under the lordship of Jesus too.
Your browser history belongs to Jesus.
Your fantasies belong to Jesus.
Your expectations belong to Jesus.
Your body belongs to Jesus.
The way you speak to your spouse belongs to Jesus.
The way you respond when your spouse is tired, grieving, afraid, recovering, insecure, aging, changing, or simply not emotionally ready belongs to Jesus.
Your bedroom does not have a sign on the door saying:
CHRIST'S LORDSHIP ENDS HERE.
No.
Especially there...
Jesus is Lord.
And perhaps that is where someone reading this suddenly feels exposed.
Because maybe the problem isn't that you desire your spouse too much.
Maybe the problem is that you stopped seeing your spouse while still desiring their body.
Maybe pornography quietly trained your expectations.
Maybe comparison poisoned your gratitude.
Maybe fantasies introduced invisible strangers into the sacred territory of your marriage.
Maybe your spouse feels as though they are competing with images they can never become.
Maybe intimacy slowly became negotiation.
Pressure.
Performance.
Resentment.
Avoidance.
Silence.
Maybe your spouse has lain inches from you while feeling profoundly alone.
And maybe nobody knows.
Church on Sunday.
Bible verse online.
Christian music playing.
Smiling family photograph.
And a marriage bleeding where nobody can see it.
This is where Jesus does something scandalously beautiful.
He doesn't merely say, "Try harder."
He comes after the heart.
That is what Matthew 5 was doing all along.
Jesus moves the conversation from external compliance into internal transformation.
Because you can technically avoid adultery while feeding an adulterous imagination.
You can remain physically faithful while emotionally cultivating someone else.
You can avoid touching another person while repeatedly undressing them in your imagination.
Jesus is not satisfied merely because your body stayed home.
He wants your heart.
But hear this carefully:
His exposure is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to repentance.
There is a difference between condemnation that says, Hide from God, and conviction that says, Come into the light.
Maybe pornography has distorted the way you see your spouse.
Bring it to Jesus.
Maybe you have pressured your spouse.
Repent.
Maybe you've withheld affection as punishment.
Repent.
Maybe you have compared your spouse's aging body to edited bodies on a screen.
Repent.
Maybe you have treated intimacy as something owed to you rather than something sacred entrusted to both of you.
Repent.
And maybe your struggle is completely different.
Maybe you have spent years believing that wanting your husband or wife was somehow spiritually inferior.
Maybe shame followed you into marriage.
Maybe nobody ever taught you the difference between sexual immorality and covenantal marital delight.
Then perhaps what you need to repent of isn't desire.
Perhaps you need to stop calling something dirty that Scripture can call good.
Jesus is not standing outside a healthy Christian marriage embarrassed by tenderness.
He created bodies.
He created covenant.
He created affection.
He created the capacity for husband and wife to delight in one another.
Sin corrupted human sexuality.
Christ did not create the corruption.
And Christ can redeem what sin distorted.
That means the biblical answer to "Can you lust after your own spouse?" requires more care than a one-word slogan.

If by "lust" you simply mean strong sexual desire for your husband or wife, Scripture gives no basis for declaring that desire inherently sinful. Proverbs and the Song of Songs make that conclusion extraordinarily difficult to sustain. Scripture can celebrate marital attraction with startling openness.

But if by "lust" you mean selfish, degrading, coercive, pornographic, unloving objectification—desire that treats your spouse as an instrument rather than a neighbor to love and a person to honor—then marriage does not baptize selfishness.
A wedding ring does not transform exploitation into holiness.
Covenant does not eliminate the command to love.
In fact, covenant intensifies it.
Husbands are commanded elsewhere to love their wives in the pattern of Christ's sacrificial love for the church.
Think about that.
Jesus did not exploit His Bride.
He gave Himself for her.
Christian marital intimacy therefore cannot finally be about:
What can I get?
It must increasingly become:
How can I love you faithfully, tenderly, joyfully, truthfully, and sacrificially before Christ?
And when two sinners learn that...
Desire changes.
Not necessarily by becoming weaker.
Sometimes by becoming deeper.
Because eventually bodies change.
Pregnancy changes bodies.
Age changes bodies.
Illness can change bodies.
Medication can change bodies.
Hormones change.
Strength changes.
Hair changes.
Skin changes.
Scars appear.
And one day the person you married may look very different from the person standing in your wedding photographs.
If your "love" was only appetite, change will terrify it.
But covenant says:
I still see you.
When the body changes...
I see you.
When life becomes exhausting...
I see you.
When intimacy requires patience...
I see you.
When your confidence disappears...
I see you.
When wrinkles replace the smooth skin I once touched...
I see you.
Because Christian marriage is not merely two bodies sharing a bed.
It is two imperfect people standing beneath the mercy of a perfect Savior, learning over decades how to love one another while Christ slowly crucifies their selfishness.
And maybe that is why this subject matters so much.
Because this was never merely an article about sex.
It was about worship.
What rules your desire?
Who defines love?
Who owns your imagination?
Who sits on the throne when nobody else can see you?
Jesus does not merely want respectable behavior.
He wants the hidden room.
The browser.
The fantasy.
The resentment.
The insecurity.
The shame.
The bedroom.
The marriage.
The heart.
All of it.
And if this article exposed something hidden in you, don't run from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Your testimony may become the evidence another wounded husband or wife desperately needed tonight that broken things are not automatically finished things.
Not as a performance.
Not to impress anybody.
But because someone scrolling quietly tonight may love Jesus while carrying questions they are terrified to ask inside a church building.
But whatever you do after reading this, don't miss the center of everything.
The answer is not simply better sexuality.
The answer is not merely a better marriage.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
Because even the purest marriage cannot save you.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Your sexual fulfillment cannot heal the deepest rebellion of your heart.
Only Christ can.
The same Jesus who exposed adultery in the heart went to a cross for adulterous hearts.
The same Jesus who commands purity offers cleansing to the impure.
The same Jesus who exposes our selfishness offers us a new heart.
At Calvary, grace did not pretend sin wasn't serious.
Grace paid for it.
And through repentance and faith, sinners are not merely taught to hide their scandals better.
They are forgiven.
Cleansed.
Redeemed.
Changed.
So bring Jesus the marriage nobody sees.
Bring Him the desire you don't understand.
Bring Him the pornography you've hidden.
Bring Him the rejection.
Bring Him the coldness.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the selfishness.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the bedroom.
Bring Him your heart.
Because perhaps the most intimate question isn't whether you still desire the person lying beside you.
Perhaps it is whether the way you desire them is learning to look more like love.
And if tonight there are two people lying on opposite sides of the same bed, both secretly wondering whether what has been broken between them can ever become beautiful again, remember this:
Jesus is still writing in rooms where everyone else thinks the story has already ended.
